title: Roger Craig reveals dementia diagnosis in Hall of Fame speech, says head injuries played role
content:
Roger Craig has been diagnosed with vascular dementia, the longtime San Francisco 49ers running back revealed Saturday during his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction speech. He said his doctors believe it could be related to the concussion he sustained in his playing career.

Craig, who turned 66 last month, attended his enshrinement in Canton, Ohio, but delivered his remarks in a prerecorded video.

“Two things can be true,” Craig said. “Football gave me opportunities beyond anything I could imagine. It helped shape the man I became. At the same time, we know more today about brain health than when I played, and I hope sharing my story encourages people to pay attention to their health and seek help when something doesn’t feel right.”

During a weekend meant to celebrate football’s history with the induction of five Hall of Famers, Craig’s announcement was a sobering reminder of the sport’s dangers.

Craig was a staple during San Francisco’s dominant run through the 1980s, winning three Super Bowls alongside fellow Hall of Famers Joe Montana, Jerry Rice and Ronnie Lott, among others. In 1985, Craig became the first player in NFL history to top 1,000 yards both rushing and receiving in a single season. In 1988, Craig won Offensive Player of the Year while also earning his lone First-Team All-Pro nod.

Craig said that his intention for sharing his diagnosis is to help others who may be experiencing a similar situation.

“The changes were gradual,” he said. “At first, they were easy to dismiss as normal aging. Over time, my family noticed it, too. Ultimately, it led us to seek answers from my doctor.”

Craig finished his NFL career with one season with the Los Angeles Raiders in 1991 and a couple of years with the Minnesota Vikings. He retired from the NFL after the 1993 season and was inducted into the Hall of Fame as a senior candidate in his 28th year of eligibility.

“I want people to know this diagnosis doesn’t define me,” Craig said. “I am still Roger Craig. I am still a father, a husband, a teammate, a friend and someone who loves this game and the people who brought it to my life. If sharing my story helps even one family or one former player, then it’s worth it. Football gave me everything.”

In the past year, the families of several former NFL players, believing head injuries had played a role in their deaths, donated their brains to be examined for Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE). The results for Marshawn Kneeland, a Dallas Cowboy defensive end who died by suicide in November, and Steve McMichael, a Hall of Fame player for the Chicago Bears who died in April of complications from ALS, were publicly revealed and showed both had CTE, which often results from repeated hits to the head.
